parts.title: What Helps Businesses Stay Upright When Their Digital Systems Are Attacked? Experts Rank the Key Factors Using Two Methods That Handle Uncertainty (Dual-Gray DEMATEL and Adaptive SWARA)
parts.abstract:
Introduction

More and more businesses are linked together through digital systems, and these networks face complicated cyber threats. To keep an organization steady, it is essential to find the things that help it bounce back from attacks, which we call cyber resilience drivers, and to decide which ones matter most. In this study, we set out to find these drivers in digital business networks, sort them into groups, and rank them by importance.

Methods

To do this, we built a step-by-step method that relies on the judgment of experts. It combines two well-known decision-making tools, called Dual-Gray DEMATEL and Adaptive SWARA. Dual-Gray DEMATEL maps how the drivers affect one another, while allowing for the fact that experts are not always sure of exact numbers. Adaptive SWARA then uses the experts' ratings to work out how important each driver is compared with the others.

Results

Our findings point to the drivers that organizations should focus on first to make them better able to withstand and recover from cyber attacks in networks of connected digital systems.

Discussion

We offer managers and researchers a structured way to help them plan for cyber resilience in businesses that are connected digitally. Our study is exploratory, and it adds a new method: it joins a way of mapping cause and effect that allows for uncertainty with a way of weighting choices that adapts to that map. Together, these support decisions about resilience when the future is uncertain.
parts.introduction_first:
Digital transformation, the shift of businesses toward digital tools and online ways of working, has completely changed how organizations run, how they deal with one another, and how they create value in today's business world (Tsai et al., 2022; Verhoef et al., 2021). More and more companies now use connected platforms, cloud computing (storing and running computers' work over the internet), and data-driven technologies, including systems powered by artificial intelligence (AI). These tools have helped organizations work more efficiently, come up with new ideas, and adapt more easily (Vial, 2019; Tsai et al., 2022).

But as businesses become more connected, they also become more exposed to cyber threats. These threats can stop operations, leak sensitive information, and spread through networks of linked businesses (Saeed et al., 2023; Chandna and Tiwari, 2023; Kure et al., 2022). Cyber attacks are becoming more clever and harder to prevent completely. So organizations need abilities that let them not only resist disruptions but also keep working and recover well when bad things happen (Bagheri et al., 2023; Kott and Linkov, 2019).
parts.conclusion:
5

Conclusion

As digital business networks become more connected and more dependent on artificial intelligence, organizations find it harder to keep working when cyber attacks disrupt them. In this study, we set out to find and rank the key drivers that help organizations stay resilient in digital systems powered by AI. We combined two decision-making methods, Dual-Gray DEMATEL and Adaptive SWARA, into one framework. This takes us beyond simply listing factors. It gives a structured picture of how 17 cyber-resilience drivers are thought to affect one another and how important each one is compared with the others.

Our analysis shows that Threat Intelligence Integration (C10) came out as the top driver. This means gathering, studying, and putting to use information about threats. Experts see it as the most important thing that makes cyber resilience possible in digital business networks. Next came Strategic Risk Assessment (C5), which means planning ahead for risks, and AI-driven Monitoring (C13), which means using AI to watch for problems. Together, these suggest that flexible ways of governing and smart ways of detecting attacks form the backbone of a resilient digital system.

The DEMATEL analysis also showed that drivers such as C10 and C5 are "net influencers." In other words, experts see them as foundational drivers that may affect many other resilience abilities further down the line. On the other hand, drivers that are "net receivers," such as those linked to recovering from incidents and keeping the business running, are more likely to improve when the influencer drivers improve.

In practice, our framework gives decision-makers a structured tool, based on expert knowledge, for spending their resources more wisely. Instead of spreading money and effort evenly across every area of resilience, organizations can use our ranking to focus on the drivers that offer the most leverage, meaning the ones that can bring improvements across their whole network of connected digital operations. The framework is especially useful where there is little hard data and decisions must rest on expert judgment in uncertain conditions.

However, these findings should be read with appropriate caution. As we explained in Section 3.6, the results come from how experts see things. They show the influence patterns experts believe in, not cause-and-effect links that have been tested with real-world data. The ranking also depends on which experts were on our panel and on the limits of the setting we studied. For this reason, we see our framework as a tool to support decisions, not as a set of rules to follow or a model that applies everywhere.

Future research could build on this work in several ways. First, larger and more varied groups of experts, from different industries, organizations of different sizes, and different countries, could show whether our findings hold more widely. Second, studies that follow the same organizations over time could show how the importance of each driver changes as new threats appear and technology advances. Third, combining our framework with real data from organizations and with measured performance results could offer ways to test and improve it. Finally, comparing our results with those from other decision-making methods may deepen our understanding of how to rank cyber-resilience drivers in digital systems powered by AI.
parts.introduction_rest:
For these reasons, cyber resilience has become a key ability that organizations need (Linkov et al., 2013; Barasa et al., 2018). By cyber resilience, we mean an organization's ability to foresee cyber disruptions, withstand them, respond to them, and recover from them, all while keeping its essential work going (Barasa et al., 2018; Kott and Linkov, 2019). Traditional cybersecurity mostly focuses on preventing attacks. Cyber resilience goes further. It focuses on adapting, keeping operations running, recovering, and learning from an organization, both during a disruption and after it ends (Annarelli et al., 2020; Bhamra et al., 2011).

This shift in thinking comes from a simple reality: in digital systems that are tightly connected, it is not realistic to expect complete protection against cyber threats. This is especially true in systems powered by AI, where threats can spread very quickly (Hausken, 2020; Kott and Linkov, 2021). So organizations need to build up their technology, their ways of working, their long-term plans, and their teamwork. These strengths help them respond quickly, make decisions together, and get their operations back on track after a cyber incident (Urciuoli, 2015; Annarelli and Nonino, 2016).

Earlier studies suggest that cyber resilience depends on several abilities that are linked to one another. These abilities work at three levels: technology, the organization itself, and the network of partners (Annarelli and Palombi, 2021; Linkov et al., 2019). At the technology level, tools such as monitoring systems, well-developed infrastructure, and security measures help organizations spot cyber incidents and keep them from spreading. These security measures include AI that detects threats and gathering information about threats (Saeed et al., 2023; Zaman et al., 2023). At the organization level, strong leadership during a crisis, flexible decision-making, and sharing knowledge help teams coordinate and adapt when disruptions strike (Duchek, 2020; Gündüzyeli, 2025). At the network level, working together, keeping a clear picture of what is happening, and exchanging information help resilience across connected ecosystems and digital supply chains, which are the chains of businesses that make and deliver a product (Tagarev and Yanakiev, 2020; Wieland and Durach, 2021). Because digital business networks are so tightly connected, a weakness in one part can quickly spread to partner organizations and supply chains. This can cause wider problems for operations and for finances (Dolgui et al., 2020; Sukachova et al., 2025).

More and more researchers are studying cyber resilience, but the research still has important gaps (Bagheri et al., 2023; Annarelli et al., 2020). Many studies mainly discuss ideas. They do not carefully examine how the drivers of resilience are connected to one another in complex digital settings, especially in digital business ecosystems powered by AI (Kott and Linkov, 2019). Earlier research has also found many factors linked to resilience. Yet relatively few studies rank these drivers by how important they are for the organization's long-term plans, while also taking into account that experts are unsure of their judgments (Moşteanu, 2020; Korucuk et al., 2022). On top of this, existing research tends to look at technology, the organization, and teamwork separately. This makes it hard to build a joined-up way of analyzing resilience in ecosystems that are connected digitally (Chandna and Tiwari, 2023; Gudla and Jamalpur, 2024). As a result, organizations still lack structured tools to help them decide. Such tools could show both how the drivers cause changes in one another and how important each driver is compared with the others, even when conditions are uncertain.

To fill these gaps, we combine two methods to rank the drivers of cyber resilience in digital business networks, paying special attention to ecosystems powered by AI. The first is Dual-Gray DEMATEL. We use it to map how the drivers cause changes in one another. It does this with "gray interval numbers," which are ranges of possible values instead of single exact numbers. This lets the method keep the uncertainty and vagueness in experts' judgments. The second is Adaptive SWARA. We then feed the map of influences into it to work out how important each driver is compared with the others. Usual versions of DEMATEL and SWARA rely on exact, single-number ratings. Our framework, by contrast, takes uncertainty into account and uses the structure of the influence map to guide the ranking.

Our study adds three things to what is known about cyber resilience in digital business networks. First, it offers a new way of thinking. It treats the drivers of resilience in AI-powered digital business networks as a whole system. In this view, resilience is not just about protecting against one-off incidents. It is an ability that keeps growing, and it covers technology, the organization, and people and their culture. This view is especially useful in ecosystems where AI plays a central role in monitoring, gathering information about threats, and adapting the response. Second, it offers a new method. It joins Dual-Gray DEMATEL, which shows how much each driver affects the others, with Adaptive SWARA, which weights the drivers, under conditions of uncertainty. This gives a more detailed way of ranking than methods that weigh choices on their own, because it builds the influence patterns that experts see directly into the weighting step. Third, it offers a practical roadmap. It shows which drivers of resilience need attention from organizations working in AI-powered digital ecosystems. It does this by looking at both how much each driver influences the network and how important it is compared with the others. This helps organizations decide where to spend their resources and build their abilities, based on evidence, in complex and connected settings.

We want to be clear about how our study fits into the field of "AI in Business." AI appears as a key part of several resilience drivers, especially C10, "Threat Intelligence Integration" (gathering, studying, and putting to use information about threats), and C13, "AI-driven Monitoring" (using AI to watch for problems). But our contribution to the method comes from combining two expert-based decision-making tools, Dual-Gray DEMATEL and Adaptive SWARA. These tools belong to a family called Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM), which means making choices by weighing several factors at once. Our contribution is not in building or using AI programs themselves. Instead, our framework uses structured expert judgment to rank the abilities that support resilience as an ongoing, whole-system process in AI-powered settings.

With this in mind, our aim is to find and rank the key drivers that shape cyber resilience in digital business settings. We carried out a systematic literature review, which is a careful search of earlier research, and checked our results with experts. In this way, we identified 17 resilience drivers and analyzed them with our framework. Our findings point to the drivers that seem to have the most influence within digital business networks. These drivers may therefore need more attention from managers and more investment in long-term plans. In this way, our study adds to research on cyber resilience and gives organizations working in digitally connected settings practical help with their decisions. To do this, we set out to answer the following research questions:
parts.methods:
3

How we did the research

3.1

How we planned the study

To find and rank the key drivers of cyber resilience in digital business networks, we used a structured approach called multi-criteria decision-making. This means making a choice when many factors have to be weighed at once. The drivers of cyber resilience are complicated, and they depend on one another. So we combined two methods into one framework: Dual-Gray DEMATEL, which maps how the drivers affect one another, and Adaptive SWARA, which works out how important each driver is compared with the others. We carried out the research in several stages, one after another (Figure 1).

First, we read widely through earlier research. We looked for drivers that other studies had reported on cybersecurity, on how organizations bounce back from trouble, and on managing risk in digital networks. From this reading we made a first list of resilience factors, and then we refined it with the help of experts. Second, we formed a panel of experts in cybersecurity, digital transformation, and the management of information systems. They checked the drivers we had found and judged how the drivers are linked to one another. We designed a questionnaire to collect their judgments on how strongly each driver influences the others. Third, we used Dual-Gray DEMATEL to study the pattern of influence that the experts saw. Experts rarely give exact numbers. Their answers are more like "medium to high influence." So we recorded each answer as a range of numbers, called a gray interval, which keeps the uncertainty in the experts' judgments instead of forcing a false sense of precision. This step let us pick out the drivers that influence others and the drivers that are influenced. Finally, we used Adaptive SWARA to work out how important each driver is and to rank them. The order in which SWARA compares the drivers was guided by the prominence values from the DEMATEL analysis, which made the ranking more structured.

Figure 1

The steps of our research.

3.2

Finding the drivers

We found the drivers of cyber resilience in two stages. We wanted the list to be complete in theory and useful in practice. First, we searched major research databases (Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect) in an organized way. We used search words such as "cyber resilience," "digital business ecosystem," "threat intelligence," and related terms. This gave us a first list of factors. We then sorted them into groups and combined them, removing duplicates and merging ideas that overlapped.

Second, a panel of ten experts checked the refined list. They came from universities and from industry, and they had backgrounds in managing cybersecurity, digital transformation, and how organizations bounce back from trouble. For each factor, they judged whether it was clear, relevant, and a good fit for digital business networks. Through this check, we removed drivers that repeated the same idea or were less relevant. This left a final set of 17 drivers of cyber resilience (Table 3). They cover technology, people and culture, and organization and strategy. They include abilities linked to AI, such as C10 (Threat Intelligence Integration) and C13 (AI-driven Monitoring).

3.3

Choosing the experts and checking their agreement

We chose the experts on purpose, rather than at random, using two rules. Each expert had to have at least 5 years of work experience in cybersecurity, information security, or digital risk management. Each also had to have been directly involved in putting cybersecurity frameworks and digital systems into practice, in overseeing them, or in checking them. The panel had 10 experts, balanced between universities and industry, so that the study would be both well grounded in theory and connected to real practice.

To check how reliable the experts' judgments were, we measured how much the experts agreed with one another. We used a score called Fleiss' kappa, which shows how much a group of people agree beyond what you would expect by chance. A score of 0 means no better than chance, and 1 means perfect agreement. Our experts scored K = 0.73, which counts as substantial agreement. This check makes the judgments we used in the later DEMATEL and SWARA analyses more reliable. Table 1 sums up the background and work experience of the experts who took part.

3.4

Dual-Gray DEMATEL

To help readers who are not specialists understand this method, here is a simple picture. Imagine you are trying to understand which parts of a complicated security system affect one another. DEMATEL (short for Decision Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory) builds an organized map of these influences, based on what experts think. For example, suppose experts believe that training employees strongly affects how fast an organization responds to an incident, and that this response speed in turn affects whether the business keeps running. Then spending money on training could set off a chain of effects across the whole resilience system.

The "Gray" version of DEMATEL accepts that experts rarely give exact numbers. They are more comfortable saying things like "medium to high influence" than committing to a precise value. So each answer is written as a range, or gray interval. For example, "Medium" influence might be written as the range [2, 3]. This uncertainty is built into the analysis on purpose, instead of being forced into a false sense of precision.

In practice, the experts first judged how strongly each driver influences every other driver, two at a time. They used a scale of words, which we turned into gray intervals (Table 1). We then combined the experts' individual judgments into one starting table, called the Initial Gray Direct-Relation Matrix. To keep the main text easy to read, we put this table in full in Appendix A. We then rescaled the table so that all its numbers could be compared fairly, a step called normalization. Through a series of calculations, we then built the Total Influence Matrix (T). This table captures both direct influences, where one driver affects another straight away, and indirect influences, where the effect passes through other drivers along the way.

From this table, we calculated two key numbers for each driver. The first is the prominence value (ri+ci). It adds together the influence a driver has on others and the influence it receives from others, so it shows how central the driver is in the whole network. The second is the relation value (ri−ci), which shows the driver's overall position. A positive relation value suggests the driver is a net influencer: experts see it as affecting others more than it is affected. A negative value marks a net receiver. We used these two numbers to draw an influence diagram (Figure 2), which maps how the experts see the cyber resilience system.

Figure 2

Map of each driver's prominence and relation.

It is important to be clear about the words we use here. In DEMATEL, the words "cause" and "effect" describe only where a driver sits in the network of influence, as judged by the expert panel. They do not mean that the driver has been shown to cause something in a real, proven way. A driver called a "cause" (or net influencer) is simply one that experts see as having more influence on the system than it receives. This suggests it might be a possible point to push on, if someone wanted to bring about change. The influence pattern we found is therefore the shared judgment of the expert panel. It should be used to support decisions, not treated as proof of real, observable cause-and-effect chains.

3.5

Adaptive SWARA

To make this method easy to understand, here is another picture. Suppose an organization has limited money and staff and needs to decide which drivers of cyber resilience to invest in first. SWARA (Step-wise Weight Assessment Ratio Analysis) gives a structured way to make that choice. Experts first rank all the drivers from most to least important. Then they compare each driver with the next one on the list, asking: "How much more important is Driver X compared to Driver Y?" The "Adaptive" version adds one extra ingredient: the results of the DEMATEL analysis, specifically the prominence values that show how central each driver is in the network of influence. This means the final importance scores reflect not only what experts prefer but also how the drivers interact within the system. The result is a ranking that takes a more complete view.

In practice, the experts ranked the 17 drivers by how important they thought each one is for making digital business networks more resilient. For each pair of drivers next to each other in the ranking, the experts then gave a ratio (sj). This ratio says how many times more important the higher-ranked driver is than the one below it. From these ratios, we calculated, one driver after another, a comparison number (kj), a recalculated weight (wj), and finally a normalized weight (qj) for each driver. A weight is a number that shows how much importance a driver gets. The key step was that we used the prominence score (ri+ci) from the DEMATEL analysis as a weighting factor during this process. This makes the SWARA method "adaptive" to the way influence flows through the system. The normalized weights give the final ranking, which shows which drivers are seen as most important for investing in.

It is essential to be clear about what these weights are and what they are not. The weights from Adaptive SWARA show the shared views and judgments of the expert panel about how important each driver is compared with the others. They are not based on data about how organizations actually perform, or on measured effects that have been checked. So this ranking should be seen as a tool to support decisions, giving structured guidance based on expert knowledge, not as firm proof of what actually works. Organizations that use these results should consider them alongside their own situation, such as how easy each driver would be to put into practice, how much money and staff they have, and the particular weak spots of their organization.

3.6

How the two methods fit together, and the limits of our study

Our framework brings together what the two methods show, to give a full picture of the drivers of cyber resilience. Dual-Gray DEMATEL shows which drivers act as central influencers in the resilience network. These are possible points where a change might set off a chain of effects. Adaptive SWARA shows which drivers matter most for the organization's strategy, which helps when money and staff are limited. Together, they give a ranking that looks at the drivers from more than one angle, balancing how much influence each driver has with how important experts think it is. This supports more careful and resilient decisions for digital business networks.

Our approach depends on experts, and it has several important limits. First, the influence pattern and the weights come from the shared views and judgments of the expert panel at one particular moment in time. They show possible points to push on, not cause-and-effect links that have been checked in real organizations. Second, the gray intervals capture the uncertainty in the experts' answers, but they do not remove the personal opinion that is always part of judgments based on words rather than measurements. Third, the framework assumes that the drivers we found are a complete enough list, and that the way they depend on one another stays the same in different organizations. These assumptions may not hold in every case. Fourth, although we chose the experts carefully, our panel is a small group, and views may differ between industries, regions, and organizations of different sizes.

For these reasons, our framework should be seen mainly as a structured tool to support decisions, not as direct proof of what actually happens in organizations. Its value is that it gives a clear and open basis for planning discussions about investing in cyber resilience. We advise people who use these results to add their own organization's data, to check how practical each driver would be to put into practice, and to keep watching as threats change over time.

3.7

Designing the questionnaire and collecting the answers

We designed a structured questionnaire to collect the experts' judgments on how the drivers of cyber resilience are linked to one another. We built it from the drivers that had been checked through the research reading and the expert screening described in the previous section. The questionnaire was designed to support the Dual-Gray DEMATEL and Adaptive SWARA methods, by letting experts give their answers even when they were unsure. It had three main parts. The first part asked about the experts themselves: their role in their organization, how many years they had worked, and their area of expertise. The second part gave short, practical definitions of each driver, so that everyone understood the drivers in the same way. The third part held tables in which the experts judged how strongly each driver influences every other driver in the cyber resilience system (see Appendix A).

Judging complicated cybersecurity relationships is often unclear and personal. So we used a gray scale of words. The experts gave their answers in set words, which we then turned into gray intervals for the calculations. This way, the uncertainty in the experts' opinions is captured openly, while they can still answer in words. Table 2 shows the scale of words we used.

Each expert judged how strongly driver i influences driver j using this scale. This gave each expert their own table of comparisons, called a gray pairwise comparison matrix. We then combined these tables into the starting table (the Initial Gray Direct-Relation Matrix) needed for the Dual-Gray DEMATEL analysis. To combine them, we took the lower and upper ends of each expert's gray intervals and combined them, giving one shared picture of the panel's judgments.

We sent the questionnaire by email to the expert panel between March 2025 and May 2025. Before the final round of answers, we tried the questionnaire out with a smaller group of experts to check that it was clear, consistent, and easy to understand. Based on their feedback, we made small changes to make the wording more precise and to reduce possible confusion. To make our methods open and easy for others to repeat, we include the full questionnaire in Appendix A. It contains the experts' background forms, the driver definitions, the comparison tables, and example questions. This extra material lets future researchers repeat our data collection and use our framework in other organizations or industries.

3.8

The Dual-Gray DEMATEL method

To study the complicated links among the drivers of cyber resilience in digital business networks, we used the Dual-Gray DEMATEL method. DEMATEL (Decision Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory) is a widely used decision-making method. It was developed to study and draw maps of how factors that depend on one another influence each other in complicated systems. However, the usual versions of DEMATEL rely on exact numbers. Exact numbers may not capture the uncertainty and vagueness of expert judgments well, especially in cybersecurity and digital business, where threats keep changing, information is incomplete, and judgments are personal.

To solve this problem, we combined DEMATEL with Gray Systems Theory. Gray theory lets uncertain expert answers be written as ranges instead of fixed numbers. This gives a more realistic picture of answers given in words when people are unsure. Unlike the usual versions of DEMATEL, which use exact numbers, our Dual-Gray DEMATEL framework keeps both the lower and upper ends of each range throughout all the calculations. Because the ranges are kept while the tables are built, rescaled, and used to work out total influence, the method gives a sturdier picture of vague expert views. This matters especially in cybersecurity and digital business, where the conditions for decisions are always uncertain and keep changing.

In this study, we collected the experts' answers as gray words that match ranges of numbers (see Table 2 in Section 3.4). We then turned these answers into Dual-Gray direct-relation matrices, which are tables holding the lower and upper ends of the influence between the drivers. We analyzed the combined tables with the Dual-Gray DEMATEL procedure, which had five main stages: (1) building the starting direct-relation tables, (2) rescaling the tables, (3) working out the total-relation tables, (4) calculating the prominence and relation values, and (5) drawing a picture of how the drivers influence one another.

Step 1. Building the gray direct-relation table

Using the experts' judgments on each pair of drivers, we built the starting gray direct-relation table, shown in Equation (1):

Z~=[[z11L,z11U]⋯[z1nL,z1nU]⋮⋱⋮[zn1L,zn1U]⋯[znnL,znnU]] (1)

where:

- zL and zU are the lower and upper ends of the gray interval,

- n is the number of drivers being judged,

- and each entry in the table shows how strongly one driver influences another.

We combined the experts' individual tables by taking the average of their numbers, which gave the shared gray direct-relation table. The combined tables for the lower ends (AL) and the upper ends (AU) are shown in Appendix B (Tables 4 and 5).

Step 2. Rescaling the gray direct-relation table

We rescaled the combined dual-gray direct-relation tables so that the strengths of influence could be compared fairly. Rescaling also meets a requirement of the DEMATEL method: the numbers must stay within a range that lets the calculations settle on a stable answer. Because our framework keeps the uncertainty in gray intervals, we rescaled the lower-end table and the upper-end table separately. Following the Dual-Gray DEMATEL approach, we based the rescaling factor on the largest row total of the upper-end table, as shown in Equation (2). This gives a cautious scaling factor that keeps the calculations stable.

where aijU is the upper end of the combined gray influence of driver i on driver j. We used the largest upper-end row total because it stands for the strongest possible influence in the system. As Equation (2) shows, using the upper end gives a cautious scaling that makes sure the DEMATEL model settles on a stable answer, while keeping the uncertainty in the gray answers. where:

- AL and AU are the combined lower-end and upper-end direct-relation tables;

- DL and DU are the matching rescaled tables;

- sL and sU are the rescaling factors for the lower and upper ends.

Rescaling squeezes every number in the tables into the range from 0 to 1. This keeps the calculations stable and stops any one driver's influence from growing out of proportion as we work out the total-relation tables. And because we kept both the lower and upper ends of the influence through the rescaling, the uncertainty in the experts' judgments stays in the cause-and-effect analysis. In this study, the largest row total of the combined lower-end table was 8.50, and the largest row total of the combined upper-end table was 12.50. So the rescaling factors were:

sL=18.50=0.1176

sU=112.50=0.0800

We then used these factors to calculate the rescaled lower-end and upper-end tables, which are shown in Appendix B (Tables B1 and B2).

Step 3: Building the total-relation tables

Once we had the rescaled gray direct-relation tables (DL) and (DU), we calculated the total-relation tables. These capture both the direct and the indirect links among the drivers of cyber resilience. In DEMATEL, the rescaled tables show only the direct influence between drivers. The total-relation tables show the combined effects that spread through the whole system. So we calculated the lower-end and upper-end total-relation tables as shown in Equations (5) and (6):

TL=DL(I-DL)-1 (5)

TU=DU(I-DU)-1 (6)

where I is the identity matrix, a 17 × 17 table with 1s along its diagonal and 0s everywhere else. TL and TU are the lower and upper ends of the total influence among the drivers. These tables include both the direct effects between drivers and the indirect effects that pass through other drivers in the network. So the total-relation tables give a full picture of how the drivers are seen to influence one another, and how strongly. The calculated lower and upper total-relation tables are shown in Appendix B (Tables B3 and B4).

Step 4: Working out the prominence and relation values

After building the total-relation tables, we calculated the prominence and relation values of the drivers of cyber resilience. These show how important each driver is overall and what role it plays in causing change in the system. We based the analysis on the total-relation table T. In the Dual-Gray DEMATEL framework, we did these calculations separately for the lower and upper total-relation tables (TL, TU), so the uncertainty stayed in the analysis throughout. For each driver i, we calculated the row total and the column total, as shown in Equations (7) and (8):

The vectors R and C were calculated as follows:

Ri=∑j=1ntij (7)

Ci=∑j=1ntji (8)

where Ri is the total of the i-th row and shows the total influence that driver i sends out, and Ci is the total of the i-th column and shows the total influence that driver i receives. From these, we calculated the prominence and relation values, shown in Equations (9) and (10):

Ri+Ci (9)

Ri-Ci (10)

The prominence value (Ri+Ci) shows how much each driver interacts with the rest of the system. Drivers with higher prominence values are considered more important, because they are strongly connected to other drivers, both by influencing them and by being influenced by them. The relation value (Ri−Ci) shows the cause-and-effect role of each driver. If (Ri−Ci) is greater than 0, the driver belongs to the cause group, meaning it mainly influences other drivers. If (Ri−Ci) is less than 0, the driver belongs to the effect group and is mainly influenced by others. The calculated prominence and relation values are shown in Table 4. Table 4 gives the Dual-Gray row and column totals of the total-relation tables (TL, TU), which match the influence each driver sends out (R) and receives (C). Using these values, we drew a Prominence-Relation Map to show the cause-and-effect relationships among the drivers of cyber resilience (Figure 2).

Step 5. Cause-and-effect analysis and drawing the map

Using the prominence and relation values, we drew a Prominence-Relation Map to show how the drivers of cyber resilience are connected (Figure 2). In this map, the horizontal axis (Ri+Ci) shows each driver's prominence, meaning how much it is involved in the system overall. The vertical axis (Ri−Ci) shows its overall cause-and-effect effect. Drivers with positive (Ri−Ci) values are called cause factors: they influence other drivers more than they are influenced. Drivers with negative (Ri−Ci) values are called effect factors: they are mainly influenced by other parts of the system. The map gives a full picture of how the drivers interact, and it makes it easier to spot the most influential cause factors, which managers can use to decide what to focus on and to plan their strategy.

The Dual-Gray DEMATEL analysis gives useful insights into how the drivers of cyber resilience are connected. In particular, the prominence values from the total-relation table show how much each driver is involved in the system, because they capture both the influence it has on other drivers and the influence it receives. DEMATEL is mainly used to study cause-and-effect links between factors, but it does not directly give importance weights that add up to one. So, to turn the influence information from DEMATEL into numbers that show how important each driver is, we used the Adaptive SWARA method in the next stage of the analysis. We used the DEMATEL prominence values to set the first order of the drivers. In this way, the SWARA process builds the pattern of influence in the system into the weighting, which gives a more structured and better-informed ranking of the drivers of cyber resilience.

3.9

The Adaptive SWARA method

After Dual-Gray DEMATEL had shown the prominence and influence pattern of the drivers of cyber resilience, we used the Adaptive SWARA (Step-wise Weight Assessment Ratio Analysis) method to work out the final weights of the drivers. SWARA is a well-known decision-making method that works out the weight of each factor by comparing how important the factors are, one step at a time. In the usual version of SWARA, the first order of the factors is taken straight from the experts' rankings. But such an order can be very personal, and it may not fully reflect how the factors are connected. To solve this problem, the adaptive version of SWARA that we used brings in the results of the Dual-Gray DEMATEL analysis. Specifically, we used the prominence values from the DEMATEL total-relation table to set the first order of the drivers of cyber resilience. Because it builds in the pattern of influence that DEMATEL revealed, Adaptive SWARA gives a weighting that is better informed about the system than the usual version of SWARA, which relies only on the experts' personal order. As Figure 1 (Research Framework) shows, Adaptive SWARA is the last stage of our framework, and it turns the DEMATEL order of prominence into weights that add up to one. The Adaptive SWARA procedure we used has five main steps, described below.

Step 1: First ranking of the drivers of cyber resilience, based on DEMATEL prominence

In the first step, we ranked the drivers of cyber resilience by their prominence values from the Dual-Gray DEMATEL analysis. The prominence value shows how important each driver is in the system overall, because it takes into account both the influence the driver has on other drivers and the influence it receives from them. As shown in Equation (11), we calculated the prominence value for each driver as follows:

Pi=Ri+Ci (11)

where Ri is the total of the i-th row of the total-relation table, showing the total influence that driver i sends out to other drivers, and Ci is the total of the i-th column, showing the total influence that driver i receives. So the prominence value Pi shows how much each driver is involved in the cyber-resilience system. Using these values, we put the drivers in order from highest to lowest to set the first order for the Adaptive SWARA procedure. To get a single number for each driver in this step, we averaged the lower and upper prominence values from the dual-gray tables. The resulting ordered list of drivers is shown in Table 5.

In the next step of the Adaptive SWARA method, we used this first order to compare how important each driver is with the driver just before it.

Step 2: Working out the comparison number

After setting the first order of the drivers of cyber resilience by their DEMATEL prominence values, the next step of the Adaptive SWARA method is to work out the comparison number. This number shows how important each driver is compared with the driver just before it in the list. Starting with the second driver in the order, the experts judged how important driver j is compared with the driver before it (j−1). This judgment is written as the comparison number sj, which shows how much less important driver j is than the driver before it. A larger value of sj means a bigger drop in importance compared with the driver before. The comparison number is calculated as shown in Equation (12):

sj=1K∑k=1Ksj(k),j=2,…,n (12)

sj: comparison number of driver j,

sj(k): the answer given by expert k for driver j,

K: number of experts,

n: total number of drivers.

where sj shows how important driver j is compared with driver (j−1) in the ordered list. The first driver in the ranking needs no comparison, so s1 = 0. Results and discussion

Our results give a picture of how experts see the cyber-resilience drivers in digital business networks powered by AI. They show how the drivers are thought to be linked to one another and how important each one is compared with the others. By combining Dual-Gray DEMATEL with Adaptive SWARA, we captured two things at once: the web of links between the drivers, and how experts would rank them when they are unsure of exact numbers.

Earlier studies stress that cyber resilience is not a single technology. Instead, it is an ability of the whole organization. It involves how the organization is governed, how ready its technology is, and how it adjusts its management as things change (Annarelli et al., 2020; Bagheri et al., 2023). Our DEMATEL results fit this view. They suggest that the drivers we studied may affect one another in a complicated web of influence, rather than working as separate, independent ways of staying resilient.

Table 4 shows which drivers experts see as having a stronger influence on the others. Some drivers seem to push on other parts of the cyber-resilience system more than others do. Others seem to depend more on the conditions around them, both in the organization and in its technology. Patterns like these match earlier research. That research suggests that resilience in digitally connected settings may grow out of the way several things work together: the organization's abilities, its rules for managing cybersecurity, and its technology (Hausken, 2020; Loonam et al., 2020). So the influence pattern we found reflects how experts think resilience abilities might develop in digital ecosystems. These are settings where many systems are tightly linked and share the same digital infrastructure (Tsai et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2020).

Table 5 shows the Adaptive SWARA results. It reveals that experts do not see all the drivers as equally important. Some drivers get relatively higher weights, meaning they count for more in the final ranking. Several drivers, however, have weights that are very close to one another. This suggests that cyber resilience in business ecosystems powered by AI may depend on a mix of abilities that support one another, rather than on one single leading factor. This fits with earlier studies. Those studies stress that good cyber-resilience strategies may need management, technology and organizational steps to work together, because cyber threats are becoming more and more complicated (Chandna and Tiwari, 2023; Saeed et al., 2023).

For this reason, the rankings in Table 6 should be read as patterns that point to priorities, based on what experts judged. They are not fixed rankings, and they may not apply everywhere. As we explained in Section 3.6, our framework is a structured tool to help people make decisions. It is not direct evidence of what actually happens inside organizations.

4.1

What our results mean for theory

Our study adds to research on cyber resilience and on digital ecosystems in several ways. First, it takes existing research further. It treats cyber resilience in digital business networks powered by AI as an ability of the whole system, shaped by linked drivers in the organization and in its technology. Earlier research has stressed that resilience is an organizational ability that lets firms foresee cyber disruptions, absorb them, and adapt to them (Barasa et al., 2018; Urciuoli, 2015). Our findings support this view. They show that the drivers of cyber resilience work within a web of influence in which they depend on one another, rather than as separate factors in the organization.

Second, our study adds something to the methods used in this field. We combined Dual-Gray DEMATEL with Adaptive SWARA to tackle two problems that often come up when researchers judge cyber resilience. One is that experts are unsure of their judgments. The other is that the things being judged affect one another. "Gray" methods let decision models handle vague and incomplete information. Such information is common in new digital settings, where exact numbers are often not available (Govindan et al., 2016; Rajesh and Ravi, 2017). A gray number is a range of possible values rather than a single exact value. By building gray numbers into the DEMATEL steps, our framework captures the uncertainty in experts' judgments more faithfully.

Third, our study moves forward research on multi-criteria decision-making, which means making choices when many factors must be weighed at once. We introduce a way of weighting drivers that is guided by how they are linked. The usual version of SWARA relies only on experts ranking the drivers by their own judgment. Our Adaptive SWARA instead starts from the influence map that DEMATEL produced. This lets the weighting reflect not only how important experts think each driver is, but also the role each driver seems to play in the web of influence. Other researchers have recently used similar combined methods for complicated cybersecurity and digital transformation problems, where many factors that affect one another must be judged at the same time (Kara et al., 2025; Sadeghi et al., 2024). We should point out, though, that the weights we get show patterns of priority that come from experts, as we discussed in Section 3.6.

4.2

What our results mean in practice

For managers, our findings offer practical guidance for organizations that want to make themselves more cyber resilient in digital ecosystems powered by AI. As digital transformation links firms, platforms and supply chain partners more closely, organizations become more exposed to cyber risks that can spread across digital networks (Tagarev and Yanakiev, 2020; Zaman et al., 2023). Our ranking results may therefore help managers see which drivers need more attention when they plan their cyber-resilience efforts.

The drivers that DEMATEL identified as net influencers may be leverage points. These are places where a change could affect many parts of an organization's resilience at once. Focusing on these drivers may help organizations make their cybersecurity rules and oversight more effective, get their technology ready, and improve how they respond. Earlier research suggests that planning ahead for cyber resilience needs coordinated investment in technology, in the organization's processes, and in the ways it manages risk (Annarelli and Palombi, 2021; Kanaan et al., 2025).

Our framework also gives decision-makers a structured tool for judging cyber-resilience priorities when things are uncertain. Many cyber-resilience challenges are judged by description and expert knowledge rather than by exact numbers. Gray-based decision methods offer practical help with planning in such uncertain settings (Asnaashari et al., 2023; Govindan et al., 2016). So our combined Dual-Gray DEMATEL and Adaptive SWARA framework may help organizations spend their resources more wisely and design balanced resilience strategies across their connected digital operations. However, as we stressed in Section 3.6, these priority results should be read as guidance that points in a direction, based on how experts see things. They should be combined with assessments made for each organization's own situation.

4.3

Limitations and future research

Our study makes useful contributions, but it also has several limitations that we should be open about. First, the findings come from experts' judgments. They therefore show the influence patterns that the particular group of experts on our panel saw, within the setting we studied. We chose the experts carefully and checked that their judgments were consistent (Section 3.6). Even so, a different group of experts, or experts from a different industry, might reach a different ranking.

Second, our study is exploratory and relies on experts to weigh many factors at once. So it does not prove cause-and-effect links between the drivers of cyber resilience. The DEMATEL results show patterns of influence that experts see, not firm proof of what causes what. For this reason, the findings should be read with appropriate caution, as we explained in Section 3.6.

Third, the gray-based approach captures the uncertainty in experts' judgments better, but the framework still depends on people's judgments. Future studies could add to our approach in several ways. They could bring in real data from organizations, use methods that test the results with numbers, or follow organizations over time to see how the drivers of cyber resilience affect how well organizations perform. Future research could also apply our framework to other industries, organizations of different sizes, or other countries, to see how widely the results hold. Finally, comparing our results with those from other multi-criteria decision-making methods may deepen our understanding of how to rank cyber-resilience priorities in digital ecosystems powered by AI.
